questions.prompt: Why is EV/Net income a meaningless ratio?
choices: Net income is too volatile to use in any multiple
Enterprise value covers all capital providers while net income is after interest, so it belongs to shareholders alone
Enterprise value is a market figure and net income is a book figure
questions.explanation: Numerator and denominator must refer to the same claimants. EV includes the lenders' claim; net income is what remains after lenders are paid.

questions.prompt: Two identical businesses differ only in that one is heavily borrowed. Which multiple compares them most fairly?
questions.explanation: EV/EBITDA measures the operating business before financing choices. P/E is distorted because interest reduces the borrower's net income.

questions.prompt: For which business does EBITDA most overstate the cash actually available to investors?
choices: A software company with minimal fixed assets
A consultancy whose main cost is salaries
A steel plant with heavy ongoing capital expenditure
A retailer that leases all its stores
questions.explanation: Adding back depreciation ignores that heavy assets genuinely must be replaced. For capital-intensive businesses the required capex is large, so EBITDA overstates distributable cash.

questions.prompt: A company trading at 20x when its peers trade at 12x is by definition overvalued.
questions.explanation: False. A higher multiple is justified by faster growth, better margins or lower risk. It is expensive only if the fundamentals do not explain the gap — which is a checkable claim.

questions.prompt: A colleague values a heavily indebted manufacturer using P/E and concludes it is cheap versus its debt-free peer. Explain what is wrong with the comparison and what you would use instead.
rubric: Identifies that P/E is distorted by leverage because interest reduces net income
Explains that equity value reflects the shareholders' residual claim, so two identically-performing businesses differ on P/E purely through financing
Recommends EV/EBITDA or EV/EBIT, and states why: enterprise value and pre-interest profit cover the same claimants
Adds the caveat that EBITDA is not cash flow, and that capital expenditure must be checked for a manufacturer
Concludes with a practical comparison that would actually settle whether it is cheap
